title: you've said it a thousand times
hookLine: you've said it a thousand times — at a table, at a funeral

lines: YOU'VE SAID IT A THOUSAND TIMES.
cards: At the end of grace, right before anyone's allowed to eat. At a funeral, quietly, along with everyone else. Amen to that, as a joke.
You've said it more times than you could count, and it's easy to hear it as the end: the prayer's over, you can open your eyes. It means something closer to the opposite.

teach.b: Amen is Hebrew, from a root, aman, that means firm. Solid. The kind of thing you can put your weight on.
The same root gives Hebrew its words for faithfulness and trust.
So amen isn't a sign-off. It's yes. That's solid.
So be it. It's old. In one scene in the books of Moses, a list of rules is read aloud to a whole people, and after each one: "And all the people shall answer and say, Amen."
A room answering yes. Then a detail that's easy to miss. In the Gospels, Jesus puts the word in a strange place: at the start.
The old English wording is "Verily, verily, I say unto you." Underneath verily is amen, amen. Usually amen came after, to agree with something already said.
He said it first, vouching for his words before he spoke them. And the last book of the Bible goes further still. It calls him "the Amen, the faithful and true witness."
Not just someone who says yes.

how: Christians say amen at the end of prayers, hymns and blessings, usually all together, as a way of saying "yes, we agree" to what was just prayed.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a name for Jesus in Revelation

s: it means "truly" or "so be it." it's a yes, not a sign-off.
Jesus sometimes started sentences with amen
"verily, verily, I say unto you": again and again in John's Gospel.
it's Hebrew, from aman: firm, solid. Greek and Latin kept it untranslated.

games.q: in an old scene, rules are read aloud to a whole people. after each one, what does the crowd do?
games.why: "and all the people shall answer and say, Amen." a room answering yes, line by line. church services still work that way.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Bring to mind one thing that's true and good in your life right now, something solid enough to put your weight on.
Stay with it. Each time you breathe out, let the answer be yes. If you pray, you can let that yes be an amen.

wordCard.voice: Amen. Firm, truly, so be it: a yes, not a goodbye. Eighth word.

orig.note: Hebrew. the Greek Gospels carry it over untranslated, and so do many languages after them.

carryVoice: Your line: let it be so. Next time a room says it, you'll know what everyone is agreeing to. Day eight.
